briefing.opening: Good day. We begin the Climate Change Daily Briefing for November 21, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 COP31 Climate Talks Face Risk of Collapse Amid Controversy Over Removal of Fossil Fuel Language
sections.content: The COP31 UN Climate Summit underway in Antalya, Türkiye, has pushed past its official deadline into overtime amid fierce discord over the omission of fossil fuel references from the draft agreement [23, 41, 45, 51]. The exclusion of fossil fuel language in the draft text drew sharp condemnation from world leaders and climate activists, with some labeling this conference the 'worst COP in history' and warning of an imminent breakdown [26, 33, 40]. With conflicting demands clashing—African nations pressing for tangible climate finance and Members of the European Parliament demanding the delivery of commitments—negotiations remain mired in a severe stalemate [35, 42, 48, 52].

sections.title: ⚠️ Deepening Climate Crisis: Warnings of 3.6°C Warming by Century's End and Marginalized Vulnerable Populations
sections.content: According to newly released climate change scenarios by the Korea Meteorological Administration, sustained high greenhouse gas emissions are projected to drive temperature increases of 3.6°C across the Korean Peninsula or globally by the end of this century [1]. Despite the acceleration of such climate disasters, only 17% of 83 surveyed countries have prioritized child hunger, underscoring how nutrition and food security measures continue to be sidelined in climate policy [2, 3]. Furthermore, the climate crisis is taking a heavy psychological toll on younger generations, with youth in Colombia's Aburrá Valley suffering from deteriorating mental health, including feelings of grief and fear [30].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Urgency of Renewable Energy Expansion in South Korea and Local Community Carbon Neutrality Actions
sections.content: The International Energy Agency (IEA) analyzed that if South Korea faithfully executes its renewable energy rollout plans, it could substantially reduce both its energy import dependence and carbon emissions [12, 14]. In particular, as renewable power emerges as a vital solution for data centers—whose electricity demand is projected to surge 13-fold by 2060—public power generation utilities are bolstering their expertise through expanded advisory mechanisms [13, 16, 19]. Alongside these developments, grassroots carbon neutrality milestones continue to mount, including the Tantan-daero 1.5 Village in Yeongdo-gu, Busan, receiving the Minister of Environment Award, and Namseoul University and Ulju-gun, Ulsan, being selected as outstanding institutions [5, 6, 10, 11].

sections.title: 🌍 International Climate Adaptation and Scientific Research in Response to Extreme Weather Threats
sections.content: In California, USA, authorities are stepping up preparedness for worst-case scenarios against the impacts of climate-intensified El Niño and atmospheric river storms on water infrastructure [27, 28]. Meanwhile, adaptation efforts leveraging natural ecosystem resilience are gaining traction, with coastal wetlands highlighted as pivotal assets for carbon sequestration and coastal defense, alongside an innovative scientific approach that tracks climate change using Himalayan marmot droppings [24, 47]. Additionally, George Washington University has enhanced public access to transparent climate data by restoring and releasing climate change indicators that were previously removed from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) website [29].

briefing.closing: Even amid the turbulent climate negotiations, scientific evidence and on-the-ground action continue to push forward. That concludes today's climate briefing.
